newsitem.title: DUBAI: Allied planes report limited Iraq radar activity.
newsitem.headline: Allied planes report limited Iraq radar activity.

text.p: Allied planes have increased sorties over an extended no-fly zone in southern Iraq and have encountered limited Iraqi ground radar activity, a U.S. military official in the Gulf said on Friday.
"Some ground radar activity was detected by air crews," the official, who requested anonymity, told Reuters.
He said the planes reported "slight Iraqi radar observation on the ground in the last 24 hours."

The official added that allied planes had "moderately" increased their sorties over the southern safe haven since it was widened on Wednesday by one degree of latitude up to Baghdad's southern suburbs.

He said allied planes were flying more missions in response to the crisis triggered by Baghdad's weekend sweep into Kurdish-run northern Iraq and the retaliatory American cruise missile strikes on Iraq this week.
The official said the allied planes, which include U.S. F15s and F16s, have not noticed any Iraqi movements "that seem to be completely out of the ordinary."
France said on Thursday it would continue to take part in allied air patrols of the southern no-fly zone but its planes would not cross the 32nd parallel despite the U.S. extension of the zone.
But the French decision has not hindered operations, the official said.
"The French issue has been incorporated into our duties. It has not had a significant impact," he said.

The CIA on Thursday said that Iraqi troops were leaving northern Iraq, but the Clinton administration said they remained a threat and refused to rule out new U.S. attacks on President Saddam Hussein's forces.
Defence Secretary William Perry told CNN that U.S. forces reserved the right to strike Iraq again if it tried to rebuild air defenses disabled by a total of 44 cruise missiles.

The Iraqi leader has vowed to ignore the exclusion zones in both northern and southern Iraq, where they have been enforced by allied warplanes since the aftermath of the 1991 Gulf war that crushed his invasion forces in Kuwait.
The United States and Iraq appeared on Thursday to back away from further confrontation but Baghdad's official media on Friday lambasted President Bill Clinton, calling him an ignorant "womaniser."

In northern Iraq, a Patriotic Union of Kurdistan official said on Friday fresh fighting erupted when the rival Baghdad-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party struck at its positions in five villages near the Iranian border.
Iraqi troops had gone into northern Iraq to support the Kurdistan Democratic Party against the other Kurdish faction.
